description: Complete configuration reference for all Colmena DAG Engine node types. Each node type documents its config fields, input ports, output ports, defaults, valid values, and validation rules.

type.description: The node type identifier that determines which execution logic is used. Must match one of the registered node types in the engine (e.g., 'llm_call', 'http_request', 'input'). This field is required for every node and is used by the DAG engine to look up the correct ExecutableNode implementation at runtime.

config.description: The node-specific configuration object. Each node type defines its own expected fields inside this object. If omitted, defaults to an empty JSON object {}. The fields available here vary by node type and are documented in each node's 'config_fields' section.

trigger_on.description: An optional condition that controls when this node executes within a looping DAG. The engine compares this value against the current '__colmena_loop_status' in the global state. The node only runs when the global status matches this value. This is essential for building cyclic graphs where certain nodes should only fire on specific loop phases — for example, an output node that only fires when the loop status is 'FINISHED', or a processing node that runs on every 'NEXT_TURN'.

max_total_calls.description: Safety limit: the maximum number of times this node can be executed during a single DAG run, regardless of which node triggered it. Once this limit is reached, the engine will skip this node for the remainder of the run. Use this to prevent infinite loops in cyclic graphs. If null (the default), the node has no execution limit.

max_calls_from.description: Fine-grained execution limits per caller node. A map where each key is a node ID and each value is the maximum number of times THIS node can be triggered BY that specific caller. This allows you to limit how many times a particular upstream node can re-trigger this node, while still allowing other callers unlimited access. Useful in complex cyclic graphs where you want to allow a loop to iterate N times from one path but unlimited from another.

from.description: The source of the edge. Can be just a node ID (e.g., 'node_a') to use that node's default output, or a dotted path (e.g., 'node_a.result') to select a specific output field. When using dotted paths, the engine extracts the specified field from the node's output JSON. You can use deep paths like 'http_node.body.access_token' to pluck nested values from a node's output.

to.description: The destination of the edge. Can be just a node ID (e.g., 'node_b') to feed into that node's default input, or a dotted path (e.g., 'node_b.prompt') to inject into a specific input port. The engine flattens the dotted path into the node's input map — for example, 'extractor.texts.slack_message' becomes the key 'texts.slack_message' in the extractor node's inputs. This is how you route data to specific named ports like 'a' and 'b' on math nodes, or 'texts.source_name' on extraction/critic nodes.

cyclic.description: Set to true to mark this edge as a backward/cyclic edge. In a normal DAG, edges must go forward (no cycles). Cyclic edges are special: they don't block the target node from executing on the first pass — the target node runs without waiting for data from this edge initially. On subsequent passes (loop iterations), the cyclic edge delivers data normally. This is essential for building looping workflows where a downstream node feeds back into an upstream node. Always pair cyclic edges with 'max_total_calls' or 'trigger_on' to prevent infinite loops.

graph_root_fields.description: Optional fields declared at the top level of the graph JSON, alongside `nodes` and `edges`. The engine propagates them to every node via the `__colmena_*` namespace, so individual nodes can read them as needed (most relevantly the `llm_call` node, which renders them into the system message). Defaults apply per-field when the key is omitted; see each field's `default` below.

timezone.description: IANA timezone identifier (e.g. `America/Bogota`, `Europe/Madrid`, `Asia/Kolkata`). Used by `llm_call` to render the temporal context block at the top of the system message: the current date/time is computed at execution time from the server clock + this timezone, then formatted as ISO 8601 (`2026-05-17T10:34:00-05:00`) with a human-readable echo. Invalid IANA strings silently fall back to `America/Bogota`, and the displayed timezone label is rewritten to match the fallback so the rendered block stays internally coherent (offset always matches the label). See developer_guide/31 (temporal context section) for the rendered format.

location.description: Free-text geographic location shown to the LLM in the temporal context block. No validation; used verbatim. Use whatever level of detail you want the LLM to see (city + country, country only, region, address, etc.). Pair with `locale` when language matters — `location` describes where the user is, `locale` declares which language to respond in.

locale.description: BCP 47 language+region tag (e.g. `es-CO`, `en-US`, `pt-BR`, `hi-IN`). Tells the LLM which language to respond in, independently of `location` — a user in `Bogotá, Colombia` might still want English replies (`en-CO`). No validation; passed verbatim to the model, which is the final arbiter of which language to use. Full BCP 47 grammar is supported (script subtags, region subtags, variants, extensions) but most graphs only need the `language-region` form.

llm_shared_fields.description: These configuration fields are shared across all LLM-powered nodes: llm_call, information_extraction, planner, critic, reactor, and the sub-components of orchestrator (planner, critic, phase_reactor, final_reactor). Each LLM node reads these from its config object.

provider.description: The LLM provider to use for this node. Determines which API endpoint and protocol will be used to communicate with the language model. Each provider has different model offerings, pricing, and capabilities. The value is case-insensitive.

mock.note: For testing only. Returns predefined responses without making real API calls.

api_key.description: The API key used to authenticate with the LLM provider. Can be provided as a literal string or as an environment variable reference using the '${VAR_NAME}' syntax (e.g., '${OPENAI_API_KEY}'). When using the '${...}' syntax, the engine resolves the value from the system environment at runtime. This is the recommended approach for production — never hardcode API keys in graph JSON files. The key must not be empty or whitespace-only.

model.description: The specific model identifier to use. If omitted, the engine uses the provider's default model. Different models within the same provider offer trade-offs between quality, speed, and cost. For example, 'gpt-4o-mini' is faster and cheaper than 'gpt-4o', while 'gemini-2.5-flash' offers fast inference for Gemini. Check each provider's documentation for available model IDs.

system_message.description: An optional system-level instruction sent to the LLM before the user prompt. System messages set the behavior, personality, and constraints for the LLM's responses. For example, 'You are a travel expert who specializes in European destinations.' The system message is only sent on the first turn of a conversation — if conversation history exists (via session_id + connection_url), the system message is skipped to avoid duplication. Supports '{{variable}}' template syntax that resolves against the node's inputs.
system_message.example: You are a helpful assistant that responds in Spanish.

verbose.description: When set to true, the node prints detailed debugging information to stdout, including the full system prompt, user prompt, and raw LLM response. Extremely useful during development and debugging to see exactly what's being sent to and received from the LLM. Should be set to false in production to avoid cluttering logs with potentially large prompts and responses.

input.name: Input Node
input.description: Provides static configuration data as output to downstream nodes. Acts as a data source that emits hardcoded values defined in its config. Supports '{{key}}' template syntax to resolve values from the DAG's global state, and allows upstream edge inputs to override individual fields. When config is empty, it acts as a pure passthrough — forwarding all injected inputs directly to its output. This is the primary way to inject initial data, configuration constants, or user parameters into a DAG flow.

data.description: The static data object to output. Can be any valid JSON value: string, number, boolean, object, or array. If present, this is the primary output of the node. Individual fields within this object can be overridden by upstream edge inputs with matching keys. If not provided, the entire config object is treated as the data source. Supports '{{key}}' and '{{key.nested}}' template syntax to dynamically resolve values from the DAG's global state at runtime.

example.question: What is the capital of France?

__payload__.description: Internal field automatically injected by the DAG engine during loop iterations or serve mode. When present, it takes absolute priority over all other config fields — the node returns this value directly without any template resolution or merging. You should never set this manually in a graph JSON file; it is managed by the engine's loop and serve mechanisms.

<any_key>.description: Any input received via edges can override the corresponding field in the config's data object. For example, if config has {"name": "default"} and an edge sends a value to 'input_node.name', the edge value replaces 'default'. Null, empty string, and empty object values from inputs are ignored (config value is preserved). Internal keys starting with '__' and 'session_id' are filtered out in passthrough mode.

output.description: The resolved data object. If 'data' was defined in config, it's the data object with templates resolved and input overrides applied. If config was empty, it's all injected inputs (minus internal keys) passed through as-is.

output.name: Output Node
output.description: Marks the terminal/final result of a DAG graph or subgraph. When the DAG engine encounters an output node, it wraps the received input in a standardized structure and flags it with '__colmena_is_output_node: true'. This flag is used by SubGraphNode to identify which node's output should be extracted and returned to the parent graph. Every DAG that needs to return a result should have at least one output node. In orchestrator-managed subgraphs, the output node is what determines the agent's result.

input.description: The value to capture as the graph's final output. Accepts any JSON value. This is typically connected to the last processing node in your graph (e.g., an llm_call's result or an http_request's body). If no input is received, the output is null.

result.description: The input value wrapped in a standardized structure: { "result": <input_value>, "extra_info": { "__colmena_is_output_node": true } }. The extra_info flag tells the SubGraphNode and DAG engine that this is the designated output.

trigger_webhook.name: Trigger Webhook
trigger_webhook.description: Entry point for external events in a DAG. In 'serve' mode, the DAG engine's HTTP server receives incoming webhook requests and injects the HTTP request body into this node via the '__payload__' field. In 'run' mode (local testing), the node uses the 'test_payload' defined in config instead. This is the standard way to make a DAG graph respond to external HTTP events. A graph should typically have exactly one trigger node as its starting point.

path.description: The HTTP endpoint path that this webhook listens on when the DAG is running in 'serve' mode. For example, '/hello' or '/webhook/process'. The DAG engine's HTTP server routes incoming requests matching this path to this trigger node. If not specified, the serve command uses a default route.

method.description: The HTTP method this webhook accepts (e.g., 'POST', 'GET'). Defines which HTTP method triggers this webhook endpoint in serve mode. Most webhooks use POST since they receive payload data in the request body.

test_payload.description: A static payload object used when running the graph locally with the 'run' command (i.e., not in serve mode). This lets you test your graph without needing to send actual HTTP requests. The test_payload simulates what a real webhook request body would contain. Can be any valid JSON structure that your downstream nodes expect.

__payload__.description: Internal field automatically injected by the DAG engine's HTTP server in 'serve' mode. Contains the raw HTTP request body from the incoming webhook call. Takes priority over test_payload. You should never set this manually.

output.description: The webhook payload, emitted directly. In serve mode, this is the HTTP request body. In run mode, this is the test_payload. The entire payload is auto-flattened, so downstream nodes can access individual fields via dotted edge paths (e.g., 'trigger.prompt').

suspend.name: Suspend (Human-in-the-Loop)
suspend.description: Pauses DAG execution and waits for human input before continuing. On first execution, the node returns a SUSPENDED status with a question for the user. The DAG engine persists the entire execution state to the database (PostgreSQL required). When the user provides an answer (via the resume API), the engine restores state and re-executes this node with the answer injected as '__colmena_resume_answer', at which point the node outputs the user's answer and execution continues downstream. This is the core mechanism for building interactive, human-in-the-loop workflows.

id.description: Stable per-question identifier used to key the resume answer payload. Required (no fallback to __node_id). Character set: [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}. The operator's --answer must reference this id with `Q[<id>]:` / `A[<id>]:` line-anchored prefixes. Renaming the surrounding node does NOT change this id, so the resume contract stays stable across graph refactors.

question.description: The question displayed to the user when execution is suspended. Should be clear and specific about what information is needed to continue. This question is included in the SUSPENDED response so the frontend or API consumer can display it to the user. Can also be provided dynamically via an input edge to the 'question' port.
question.example: Do you approve this flight booking for $450?

question_type.description: Question kind. `open` accepts free-form text. `choice` exposes an `options` array as a UX hint — the parser does NOT whitelist against options, so the operator may answer with any of the suggested options OR free text.

options.description: Suggested answer values for `question_type: "choice"`. UX suggestion list, NOT a whitelist — the resume parser accepts any free-text answer regardless of whether it appears in `options`. Use this to give the frontend / LLM quick-pick hints without forcing the operator into a closed set.

question.description: An optional dynamic question provided via an upstream edge. If provided, overrides the question defined in config. This allows you to generate context-dependent questions based on earlier processing results.

__colmena_resume_answer.description: Automatically injected by the DAG engine when resuming from a suspended state. Contains the user's answer. You never set this manually — it's managed by the engine's resume mechanism.

answer_received.description: On resume: the user's answer value. On first execution (suspend): not available — the node returns a SUSPENDED status object instead. Downstream nodes should connect to this port to receive the human input.

resume_answer_format.description: Operators (or LLMs) write the answer using Q[<id>]:/A[<id>]: prefixes anchored at line start. The <id> is the config.id of this suspend node. Multi-line answers are preserved between A[<id>]: and the next prefix or end of input. The question echo is for human readability; the parser does not validate it. For choice questions, options are UX suggestions — any free-text answer is accepted. Format is canonical and shared with `secure_suspend`.

minimal_open.description: Minimal suspend: free-text approval gate between an input and a log.

choice_with_options.description: Choice question with UX hint options. Free-text answers are still accepted — options are not a whitelist.
choice_with_options.resume_answer:
Q[pick_env]: ¿A qué entorno hacemos deploy?
A[pick_env]: production

dynamic_question_from_upstream.description: Question generated upstream and injected via edge into the suspend node's `question` input port. Edge value overrides config.question; config.id is unchanged.

test_graphs.what_it_exercises: Minimal suspend between mock_input and log — smoke test.

loop_controller.name: Loop Controller
loop_controller.description: Controls the lifecycle of a cyclic/looping DAG by determining whether to continue iterating (NEXT_TURN), stop (FINISHED), or pause for user input (SUSPENDED). This node is the decision point in looping workflows — it reads the current loop status (typically set by a Python script or other logic node) and signals the engine accordingly. The output includes a '__colmena_loop_status' field that the engine reads to decide whether to re-execute the graph from the beginning or terminate. Essential for building multi-turn conversational agents, iterative processing pipelines, and any workflow that needs to repeat.

loop_status.description: The loop continuation status. Determines what the DAG engine does after this node executes. 'NEXT_TURN' tells the engine to re-execute the entire graph from the start with updated state (the output of this iteration becomes the input of the next). 'FINISHED' tells the engine the loop is complete and execution should stop. 'SUSPENDED' pauses execution and waits for user input. Can be overridden by the 'loop_status' input port or forced to SUSPENDED by the 'suspend_flag'.

suspend_flag.description: When set to true, forces the loop status to 'SUSPENDED' regardless of the 'loop_status' value. This is a convenience override — instead of changing the loop_status string, you can set this boolean flag to trigger a suspension. Useful when a downstream critic or reviewer node decides that user input is needed.

question.description: The question to present to the user when the loop is suspended. Only included in the output when the effective status is 'SUSPENDED'. Should clearly communicate what information the user needs to provide for the loop to continue.
question.example: Are you satisfied with the results, or should we refine the search?

all_tasks.description: The final payload to include in the output when the loop status is 'FINISHED'. Typically contains the accumulated results from all loop iterations. This becomes the 'final_result' in the output, allowing downstream nodes (like an output node) to access the complete loop results.

loop_status.description: Dynamic loop status provided by an upstream node. Overrides the config value. Typically set by a Python script or logic node that evaluates whether the loop should continue.

suspend_flag.description: Dynamic suspend flag. When true, overrides loop_status to SUSPENDED.

question.description: Dynamic question for the SUSPENDED state.

all_tasks.description: Dynamic final payload for the FINISHED state.

output.description: A JSON object containing: '__colmena_loop_status' (the effective status string), optionally 'question' (when SUSPENDED), and optionally 'final_result' (when FINISHED). The DAG engine reads '__colmena_loop_status' to decide whether to loop again, stop, or suspend.

subgraph.name: SubGraph
subgraph.description: Executes a child DAG graph in an isolated session. The child graph runs independently with its own session ID (derived from the parent's), its own state, and its own execution lifecycle. All non-internal inputs received by this node are passed to the child graph as its initial state. The child graph's output node result is extracted and returned as this node's output. If the child graph suspends (e.g., via a suspend node), the suspension bubbles up to the parent graph. This is the core building block for the orchestrator's multi-agent architecture — each agent is a subgraph. Can also be used standalone to modularize complex graphs.

child_graph_path.description: File system path to a JSON file containing the child graph definition. The file must contain a valid Colmena graph JSON with 'nodes' and 'edges'. The path can be absolute or relative to the working directory. At least one of 'child_graph_path' or 'child_graph_inline' must be provided. Use this when the child graph is stored as a separate file (good for reusability and maintenance).

child_graph_inline.description: An inline child graph definition embedded directly in the config. Must contain 'nodes' and 'edges' keys, just like a standalone graph JSON file. At least one of 'child_graph_path' or 'child_graph_inline' must be provided. Use this when the child graph is simple and tightly coupled to the parent (common in orchestrator agent definitions).

__agent_name.description: Internal field injected by the OrchestratorNode when this subgraph runs as an agent. Contains the agent's name/ID. Used for emitting boundary events in the event stream so the parent can track which agent produced which output. You should never set this manually.

<any_key>.description: All non-internal inputs (keys not starting with '__colmena_' or '__node_id') are passed to the child graph as its initial global state. This is how the parent graph injects context, prompts, and configuration into the child graph.

result.description: The child graph's output, extracted from the node flagged with '__colmena_is_output_node: true'. If the child graph suspends, this contains the SUSPENDED status object which bubbles up to the parent.

router.name: Router
router.description: Routes the input to one of N declared branches. Mode 'llm_direct': the LLM reads each branch's description and picks one by name. Mode 'extract_and_route': the LLM first extracts a JSON object against an inline schema, then declarative 'when' rules pick the branch in declaration order (first match wins). Each branch is a named output port; only the selected port emits a non-null payload, all others emit null. Each branch may optionally declare a 'subgraph' (path or inline) that runs internally before emission. Fails fast (no default branch) when no rule matches or the LLM picks an unknown branch — error embeds the extracted JSON for diagnostics. Always emits an additional '__decision' output port with { selected_branch, reason?, extracted? } for logging.

mode.description: Routing strategy. 'llm_direct' = LLM picks a branch by name from descriptions. 'extract_and_route' = LLM extracts JSON against 'schema', then 'when' rules per branch decide.

schema.description: Inline schema (same format as output_parser.schema). Required when mode = 'extract_and_route'; forbidden in 'llm_direct'.

instructions.description: Optional extra rules appended to the system message (mode A: routing rules; mode B: extraction rules).

branches.description: Non-empty array of branch declarations. Each entry: { name (required, ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$), description? (required in mode A, forbidden in mode B), when? (required in mode B, forbidden in mode A), subgraph? }. Names must be unique. Branches are evaluated in declaration order (first match wins).

input.description: The text or value to route. Non-string values are pretty-printed as JSON. Empty input (null/""/[]/{}) fails the node — there is no silent skip.

<branch_name>.description: One port per declared branch. Emits the payload ({ input, extracted? }) only on the selected branch; emits null on all others. If the selected branch declares a 'subgraph', the subgraph's output is emitted instead of the raw payload. SUSPENDED bubbles up through this port when the subgraph suspends.

__decision.description: Always emitted on success: { selected_branch, reason?, extracted? }. Use for logging, audit trails, or as a debug output. On routing failure, the extracted JSON is embedded in the node error message (no partial __decision is emitted).

branches.description: User asks a question that can be answered with general knowledge.

branches.description: User asks something that requires human follow-up.

log.name: Log (Debug)
log.description: A debug/inspection node that prints its input to stdout (console) and passes it through unchanged. Useful for inspecting intermediate values during graph development and debugging. Does not modify the data — whatever goes in comes out exactly the same. Accepts input from common keys ('input', 'result', 'output') or, if none of those are present, aggregates all inputs into a single object for display.

input.description: The primary input to log. The node also checks 'result' and 'output' keys as fallbacks. If none of these standard keys are present but other inputs exist, all inputs are combined into a single object and logged together.

output.description: Pass-through of the input value. The exact same value that was logged is emitted as output, allowing you to insert log nodes anywhere in your graph without disrupting data flow.

mock_input.name: Mock Input
mock_input.description: A test helper node that emits its entire config object as output without any transformation. Unlike the Input node, MockInput ignores all upstream inputs and simply returns whatever is in its config. Useful for unit testing specific parts of a graph by injecting fixed test data. The output is the raw config value — no wrapping in {"output": ...}.

<any_key>.description: Any key-value pair defined in config becomes part of the emitted output. For example, { "x": 10, "y": 5 } makes the entire object { "x": 10, "y": 5 } the node's output. Downstream nodes can then access individual fields via dotted edge paths (e.g., 'mock.x').

<raw_config>.description: The entire config object emitted as-is. No default_output key — the output is the raw config value directly.

add.name: Add
add.description: Performs addition of two numbers (a + b). Both operands must be provided via input edges — this node has no config fields. The inputs must be numeric values (integer or float). Returns the sum in a standardized { "output": result } structure.

a.description: The first operand (addend). Must be a valid JSON number. Connect an upstream node's numeric output to this port using an explicit edge like { "from": "source.value", "to": "add.a" }.

b.description: The second operand (addend). Must be a valid JSON number. Both 'a' and 'b' are required — the node returns an error if either is missing or non-numeric.

output.description: The sum: a + b. Always a JSON number (float64 internally).

subtract.name: Subtract
subtract.description: Performs subtraction of two numbers (a - b). Both operands must be provided via input edges. Returns the difference.

a.description: The minuend (the number being subtracted from). Must be a valid JSON number.

b.description: The subtrahend (the number to subtract). Must be a valid JSON number.

multiply.name: Multiply
multiply.description: Performs multiplication of two numbers (a * b). Both operands must be provided via input edges. Returns the product.

a.description: The first factor (multiplicand). Must be a valid JSON number.

b.description: The second factor (multiplier). Must be a valid JSON number.

divide.name: Divide
divide.description: Performs division of two numbers (a / b). Both operands must be provided via input edges. Returns an error if b is zero (division by zero is not allowed). Returns the quotient as a floating-point number.

a.description: The dividend (the number being divided). Must be a valid JSON number.

b.description: The divisor (the number to divide by). Must be a valid JSON number and must NOT be zero. A division by zero produces a 'DivisionByZero' error.

output.description: The quotient: a / b. Always a float64 value.

exponential.name: Exponential (Power)
exponential.description: Raises a base number to a given exponent (base^exponent). The base is provided via the 'input' port, and the exponent is defined in config. Uses floating-point exponentiation (powf), so fractional exponents work (e.g., exponent 0.5 computes square root).

exponent.description: The power to raise the input base to. Can be any numeric value: positive integers for standard powers (2 = square, 3 = cube), 0.5 for square root, negative values for reciprocals (e.g., -1 computes 1/base). This is defined in config because the exponent is typically a fixed parameter of the node's role in the graph.

input.description: The base value to raise to the power of 'exponent'. Must be a valid JSON number. Connected via the default input port (e.g., { "from": "source", "to": "exp" }).

output.description: The result: input^exponent. A float64 value.

http_request.name: HTTP Request
http_request.description: Makes HTTP requests to external APIs and returns the response. Supports GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH methods with configurable headers, query parameters, request body, and authentication. All string values in config support '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable resolution — essential for injecting API keys and tokens securely. Input values override config values (inputs take priority). When used as an LLM tool (via tool_configurations), extra non-reserved input keys are automatically added as query parameters, enabling the LLM to control request parameters dynamically. NEW: any string value in the body that matches the pattern '$attachment:<storage_key>' is resolved by reading bytes from OutputStorageRepository and replaced with 'data:<mime>;base64,...'. This lets agents ship generated images/audio to external endpoints without ever seeing the raw bytes. MULTIPART MODE: When the resolved Content-Type header starts with 'multipart/', the body is interpreted as a multipart form. Each top-level field's value is treated as: a URL string (HEAD-validated then streamed in), a $attachment:<storage_key> string (streamed from OutputStorageRepository), a plain string (text part), an array (expanded to N parts under the same field), or an explicit object with url/attachment/value + optional filename/content_type. Number and boolean values are coerced to text. Null omits the field. Limits are configurable per request.

base_url.description: The base URL for the HTTP request (protocol + domain + optional base path). For example, 'https://api.example.com' or 'https://test.api.amadeus.com'. Combined with 'endpoint' to form the full URL. Trailing slashes are automatically handled. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax for dynamic URL resolution.

endpoint.description: The URL path appended to base_url. For example, '/v1/shopping/flight-offers' or '/users'. Leading slashes are automatically handled — you can use '/endpoint' or 'endpoint' and both work. The full request URL is constructed as '{base_url}/{endpoint}'. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax.

method.description: The HTTP method to use for the request. Determines the type of operation: GET for fetching data, POST for creating resources or sending data, PUT for updating resources, DELETE for removing resources, PATCH for partial updates. The value is case-insensitive internally but conventionally written in uppercase.

headers.description: Custom HTTP headers to include in the request. A key-value map where keys are header names and values are header values. Header values support '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax. Common headers include 'Content-Type' (usually 'application/json'), 'Accept', and custom API-specific headers. A default 'User-Agent: colmena-http-node/0.1' is always added. Headers from inputs are merged on top of config headers (input headers override config headers with the same key).

query_params.description: Query parameters appended to the URL. A key-value map that gets serialized as URL query string (e.g., '?key=value&key2=value2'). Both config and input query_params are sent (input params are added on top of config params). When this node is used as an LLM tool, any extra non-reserved input keys that are primitive values (string, number, boolean) are also automatically added as query parameters, allowing the LLM to dynamically control the request.

body.description: The request body. Can be a JSON object (sent as application/json with automatic serialization) or a string (sent as raw text). Typically used with POST, PUT, and PATCH methods. Input body overrides config body. When used as an LLM tool with the '$DYNAMIC' placeholder system or node_schema, the LLM can generate individual body fields that get merged with fixed values.

bearer_token.description: A convenience field for Bearer token authentication. When provided (typically via an input edge from an auth node), the node automatically sets the 'Authorization: Bearer {token}' header. This saves you from manually constructing the Authorization header. Commonly used with OAuth2 flows where a separate auth node obtains the access token.

authorization.description: A custom Authorization header value. Unlike 'bearer_token' which automatically prepends 'Bearer ', this field sets the Authorization header to exactly the value provided. Use this for non-Bearer auth schemes like Basic auth ('Basic base64encoded'), API keys ('ApiKey xyz'), or custom schemes.

secure.description: Internal Colmena flag used by the Secure Values system. When present, indicates that this request may contain injected secure values. This flag is NEVER sent to external APIs — it's stripped from the request before sending. Used internally to control logging behavior (preventing accidental exposure of credentials in logs).

max_file_size_bytes.description: Hard cap per file part in multipart mode. Validated against Content-Length (URL parts) or size_bytes (attachment parts).

max_parts.description: Maximum total parts (file + text) per request in multipart mode.

url_download_timeout_secs.description: Timeout (seconds) for HEAD pre-flight and GET connect/headers phase of URL parts in multipart mode. Does NOT bound body transfer duration.

allow_http_urls.description: When false, plain http:// URLs in multipart parts are rejected (SSRF mitigation). Set true to permit insecure URLs.

headers.description: Dynamic headers. Merged on top of config headers.

body.description: Dynamic request body. Overrides config body.

query_params.description: Dynamic query params. Added on top of config params.

<extra_keys>.description: Any non-reserved input keys with primitive values (string, number, boolean) are automatically added as query parameters. This enables LLM tool calling to dynamically control request parameters.

status.description: The HTTP response status code (e.g., 200, 404, 500). Always present in the output.

body.description: The HTTP response body, parsed as JSON if possible. If the response is not valid JSON, this is null. This is the default output port — downstream nodes connected without specifying a field get this value.

secure_suspend.name: Secure Suspend (Secret Collection)
secure_suspend.description: Pausa el DAG y pide al usuario uno o más secretos en una sola pausa. Persiste cada valor cifrado en la tabla de secure_value_mappings y devuelve solo handles `<sv_<name>>`. El valor real nunca aparece en outputs ni en logs ni en el contexto del LLM. Soporta uso como nodo top-level del DAG o como LLM tool en `tool_configurations`.

secrets.description: Lista de objetos { question, name }. Mínimo 1, máximo 8. Cada `name` debe matchear ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,63}$ y ser único dentro de la lista. El `name` cumple doble rol: identifica el handle persistido (`<sv_<name>>`) y es el id usado por el operador en la respuesta de resume (formato `Q[<name>]:` / `A[<name>]:`). El `question` es human-readable y NO se valida contra el echo en el resume — el parser binda por id, así que el LLM puede reformular o traducir libremente.

id.description: ID estable del bloque de preguntas. Default: el __node_id del nodo. Las questions emitidas tienen IDs de la forma `<id>__1`, `<id>__2`, ...

secrets.description: Array dinámico de { question, name } provisto por un nodo upstream. Útil cuando el LLM decide en runtime qué secretos pedir.

__colmena_session_id.description: Inyectado automáticamente por el engine. Scope de los handles persistidos.

__node_id.description: Inyectado automáticamente por el engine. Usado como base ID si config.id no está presente.

__colmena_resume_answer.description:
Inyectado automáticamente al reanudar. Formato: `pregunta
valor
pregunta
valor`. Nunca se configura manualmente.

handles.description: Mapa { <name>: '<sv_<name>>' } con un handle por secreto. Solo disponible en el resume-path. El valor real nunca es expuesto.

status.description: Valor fijo 'resumed'. Solo disponible en el resume-path.

__colmena_status.description: Valor 'SUSPENDED' en el suspend-path. Señaliza al engine que pause la ejecución.

questions.description: Array [{ id, question, type: 'secret', options: null }, ...] en el suspend-path. Una entrada por ítem en config.secrets, con IDs <base>__1, <base>__2, ...

resume_answer_format.description: Resume answers are keyed by the secret's `name`. Order does not matter — the parser binds by id. Multi-line answers preserved between A[<name>]: and the next prefix or end of input. Format is canonical and shared with the `suspend` node. Only open questions are supported (no choice in this iteration).

socketio_request.name: Socket.IO Request
socketio_request.description: Connects to a Socket.IO server, emits an event with a JSON payload, and receives the response via acknowledgment callback or a separate server event. Supports two response patterns: ack mode (default — server responds via Socket.IO acknowledgment callback) and wait-event mode (set 'wait_event' to listen for a named server event instead). Supports namespaces, cookie-based authentication, custom headers, and configurable transport (WebSocket, polling, or auto). All string values in config support '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable resolution — essential for injecting API URLs and tokens securely. Input values override config values (inputs take priority). Each execution creates a fresh connection, emits the event, collects the response, and disconnects.

url.description: The Socket.IO server URL (protocol + domain + optional path). For example, 'https://api.example.com' or 'http://localhost:3000'. The client connects to this URL and performs the Socket.IO handshake. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax.

namespace.description: The Socket.IO namespace to connect to. Namespaces allow multiplexing multiple communication channels over a single connection. The default namespace is '/'. Common examples: '/canvas', '/chat', '/notifications'. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax.

event.description: The event name to emit to the server. This is the Socket.IO event identifier that the server listens for. For example, 'load_canvas_state', 'create_node', 'ping'. The value is sent as-is to the server.

payload.description: The JSON payload sent along with the event. Can be any valid JSON value (object, array, string, number, boolean, null). All string values within the payload are recursively resolved for '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable references. If omitted, an empty object {} is sent. Input payload overrides config payload entirely (no merging).

headers.description: Custom HTTP headers sent as opening headers during the Socket.IO handshake. A key-value map where keys are header names and values are header values. Header values support '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax. These are passed via the underlying HTTP upgrade request. Input headers override config headers with the same key.

cookies.description: Cookie string sent as the 'Cookie' opening header during the Socket.IO handshake. This is a convenience field — equivalent to setting headers: { "Cookie": "..." } but shorter. Commonly used for session-based authentication. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax.

wait_event.description: When set, the node switches from ack mode to wait-event mode. Instead of using the Socket.IO acknowledgment callback for the response, the node listens for this named server event. This is useful when the server responds by broadcasting a separate event rather than acknowledging the original emit. For example, setting wait_event='canvas_state_loaded' will emit the event and then wait for a 'canvas_state_loaded' event from the server.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds for the response (ack callback or wait_event). If the server does not respond within this time, the node returns an error envelope: { success: false, event, error: 'Timeout...' }. Default is 10000 (10 seconds). Increase for slow operations or large data transfers.

transport.description: The transport type for the Socket.IO connection. 'any' (default) lets the client choose automatically (usually starts with polling, upgrades to WebSocket). 'websocket' forces WebSocket-only. 'polling' forces HTTP long-polling only.

pre_events.description: Optional sequence of events to emit on the SAME connection BEFORE the main event. Useful for servers that scope state per-socket (e.g., room subscriptions, sessions). Each item is an object: { event: string (required), payload?: any (default {}), wait_event?: string (optional, listen for a separate ack event), timeout_ms?: integer (optional, falls back to the node's timeout_ms) }. String values inside each item's payload support '${VAR_NAME}' resolution. Pre-events are executed sequentially in order. If any pre-event fails (timeout, server exception, channel error), the node aborts: it disconnects, does NOT emit the main event, and returns an envelope with success=false, failed_pre_event=<name>, error=<msg>, and pre_responses listing the pre-events that did complete. On success the output includes pre_responses: [{event, response}, ...] alongside the main response. Backward-compatible: if absent or empty, behavior is identical to the legacy single-event flow.

timeout_ms.description: Dynamic timeout in ms. Overrides config.

pre_events.description: Dynamic pre_events sequence. Overrides config entirely.

success.description: Whether the request completed successfully. True when the server responded via ack or wait_event. False on timeout, server exception, or channel error (including pre-event failure).

event.description: The event name that was emitted. Echoed back for identification when multiple socket tools are in use.

response.description: The server response data. In ack mode, this is the acknowledgment payload. In wait-event mode, this is the data from the waited event. This is the default output port — downstream nodes connected without specifying a field get this value. On error, this field is absent and 'error' contains the error message.

pre_responses.description: Only present when pre_events were configured. Array of { event: string, response: any } objects in the order the pre-events executed. On a pre-event failure, contains only the entries that completed before the failing one.

failed_pre_event.description: Only present when a pre_event failed. Names the pre-event whose ack/wait_event timed out or whose server emitted an exception. The main event is NOT emitted in this case.

error_envelope.description: On failure (timeout, server exception, channel error), the node returns an error envelope instead of throwing. This allows downstream nodes to handle errors gracefully. When pre_events are involved, the envelope additionally carries failed_pre_event (if a pre-event failed) and pre_responses (the entries that did complete).

schema.exception: any (optional, present only for server-side exceptions caught via the 'exception' event)
schema.failed_pre_event: string (optional, present when a pre_event failed — the main event was NOT emitted)
schema.pre_responses: array (optional, present when at least one pre_event completed)

sql_query.name: SQL Query
sql_query.description: Executes PostgreSQL queries with granular permission control and a hybrid validation pipeline (static rules + optional LLM critic). Designed primarily as an LLM tool: configure connection, permissions, and guardrails as fixed values in node_schema, exposing only the 'query' parameter to the LLM. Supports SELECT (incl. WITH/CTE), INSERT (single- and multi-row), UPDATE, DELETE (WHERE required), CREATE TABLE, CREATE FUNCTION (with mandatory COMMENT ON), and COMMENT ON, controlled via permission presets (read_only, read_write, full) with an optional deny list. Always blocked regardless of preset: DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, CREATE SCHEMA, CREATE INDEX, CREATE VIEW, GRANT, REVOKE — manage these via migrations. Queries are parsed with sqlparser's PostgreSQL dialect; multi-statement scripts are validated per-statement (so `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE x;` is rejected). Unparseable input returns a `Failed to parse SQL: …` error with no string-matching fallback. Features automatic schema introspection for LLM context injection, a sandbox schema for agent-created functions, runtime limits (statement_timeout, work_mem, max_rows applies to SELECT only), and multi-tenant Row-Level Security (RLS) via tenant_user_id, tenant_column, and auto_rls fields.

connection_url.description: PostgreSQL connection URL. Supports ${ENV_VAR} syntax for environment variable resolution.

setup_sql.description: Operator-authored DDL + seed run once at node init to bootstrap the database environment (schema, tables, seed rows). Operator trust-level: bypasses the LLM validator. Runs idempotently on every init — MUST be written idempotent (CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING). Executed as one atomic transaction; any failure rolls back and hard-fails init. The LLM never sees it.

permissions.description: Permission configuration controlling what SQL operations the agent can perform. Defaults to read_only if omitted.

preset.description: Permission preset: 'read_only' (SELECT only), 'read_write' (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE), 'full' (all including DELETE and CREATE FUNCTION).

deny.description: Operations to deny from the preset (e.g., ['delete'] with read_write preset).

allowed_schemas.description: List of PostgreSQL schemas the agent can access. Operations against other schemas are blocked.

sandbox_schema.description: Schema where the agent can create functions and temporary tables. Must be in allowed_schemas.

tenant_user_id.description: User ID for RLS multi-tenancy. Supports ${ENV_VAR} resolution. When set, runs SET app.current_user_id before every query.

tenant_column.description: Column name used for tenant isolation in RLS policies.

auto_rls.description: When true, auto-creates RLS policies during initialization and after CREATE TABLE. Tables with tenant_column get tenant isolation; tables without get read-only.

create_schemas_if_missing.description: When true (default), the node checks each schema in allowed_schemas at initialization and creates the ones that don't exist (operator-driven provisioning — the names come from fixed config, not the LLM). Existing schemas are left untouched. If a missing schema cannot be created (e.g. the database role lacks CREATE privilege), node initialization fails. Set to false to keep the legacy validate-only behavior. Note: LLM-issued CREATE SCHEMA in a query stays blocked regardless of this flag.

runtime_limits.description: Runtime limits applied to each query execution.

max_rows.description: Maximum number of rows returned by SELECT queries. Results exceeding this are truncated.

statement_timeout_ms.description: Maximum query execution time in milliseconds.

work_mem_mb.description: PostgreSQL work_mem setting in MB for sort/hash operations.

guardrail_enabled.description: Enable static validation rules (always recommended). Checks for dangerous patterns like DELETE without WHERE, unauthorized operations, etc.

guardrail_llm.description: Optional LLM critic configuration. When enabled, a second LLM reviews each query for security risks and optimization opportunities before execution.

enabled.description: Whether to activate the LLM critic.

model.description: Model to use for the critic.

api_key.description: API key for the critic LLM. Supports ${ENV_VAR} syntax.

query.description: The SQL query to execute. When used as an LLM tool, this is the parameter the LLM provides.

output.description: For SELECT: array of row objects. For mutations: { rows_affected: N }. For CREATE FUNCTION: { created: true, name, schema }.

row_count.description: Number of rows returned or affected.

truncated.description: Whether results were truncated due to max_rows limit.

python_script.name: Python Script
python_script.description: Executes arbitrary Python code within the DAG. All input values received via edges are injected as global Python variables (e.g., if input has 'x': 10, the Python code can use 'x' directly), EXCEPT the reserved keys 'code', 'sandbox_mode', and 'sandbox_timeout_secs' which are consumed as node configuration and not exposed to the script. The Python script must assign its result to a variable named 'output' — this variable is extracted and returned as the node's output (returns null if 'output' is not defined). Supports standard library imports (math, json, etc.). Code can be provided via config or overridden via the 'code' input port (input takes priority). Markdown code block wrappers (```python...```) are automatically stripped, making it safe to receive code from an LLM. Optional sandbox mode ('restricted') performs AST validation against an import whitelist + banned-builtin list and enforces a timeout — designed for LLM-generated code. Runs in a dedicated blocking thread via PyO3 (`tokio::task::spawn_blocking`) to ensure GIL safety with the async runtime.

code.description: The Python code to execute. Can be a single expression (e.g., 'output = x * y + 2') or a multi-line script with imports, functions, loops, etc. The code runs in an isolated namespace where all input values are available as variables. You MUST assign the result to a variable called 'output' — this is the convention the node uses to extract the return value. If 'output' is not defined after execution, the node returns null. The code input port takes priority over this config field, allowing LLMs or upstream nodes to dynamically provide code. INTRINSIC LIMITATION (Python → JSON): the value of 'output' is converted to JSON before leaving the node, so it must be JSON-serializable — only dicts with STRING keys are valid (e.g. `output = {'a': b}` works, `output = {a: b}` fails when `a` is a number); types like set, bytes, datetime, Decimal, custom classes, NaN/Infinity, and circular references must be coerced explicitly (str(), list(), .isoformat(), .decode(), etc.). See docs/developer_guide/26_python_node.md → 'The Python ↔ JSON Boundary' for the full table and workarounds.

sandbox_mode.description: Execution sandbox level. 'none' (default) runs code with full Python access — safe for trusted code. 'restricted' validates the code via AST before execution: only whitelisted imports are allowed (math, json, re, datetime, collections, itertools, functools, string, decimal, statistics) and banned builtins (open, exec, eval, compile, __import__) are blocked. Use 'restricted' whenever the code is generated by an LLM or provided by an untrusted source.

sandbox_timeout_secs.description: Maximum execution time in seconds. Only applies when sandbox_mode is 'restricted'. If the script exceeds this limit, the node returns a SandboxTimeout error to the caller. KNOWN LIMITATION: a tight Python loop (e.g., 'while True: pass') holds the GIL and cannot be cancelled by the timeout — the caller receives the error correctly, but the underlying blocking-pool thread remains occupied until the process restarts. In long-running 'serve' mode this can exhaust the blocking thread pool over time. Avoid for fully untrusted multi-tenant code; for LLM-generated code (the primary use case), the AST check + timeout combo is sufficient because LLM-written tight loops are rare and recoverable. Minimum recommended value: 2; increase for scripts that process large datasets.

code.description: Dynamic Python code that overrides the config code (reserved key, NOT injected as a Python variable). Useful when the code is generated by an LLM or computed by an upstream node. Markdown code block wrappers are automatically stripped.

sandbox_mode.description: Reserved key. Overrides the config sandbox_mode for this execution. NOT injected as a Python variable. Same valid values and semantics as config.sandbox_mode ('none' | 'restricted').

sandbox_timeout_secs.description: Reserved key. Overrides the config sandbox_timeout_secs for this execution. NOT injected as a Python variable. Same semantics as config.sandbox_timeout_secs (only enforced when sandbox_mode is 'restricted').

<any_key>.description: Every input key-value pair (other than the reserved keys 'code', 'sandbox_mode', 'sandbox_timeout_secs') is injected as a Python variable accessible in the script. For example, if an edge sends 'x': 10, the Python code can reference 'x' directly. Complex JSON objects and arrays are converted to Python dicts and lists respectively.

<raw>.description: The node emits the RAW value of the Python 'output' variable, NOT a wrapper object. If the script does 'output = 52', the node's output is the number 52. If the script does 'output = {"count": 5}', the node's output is the dict {"count": 5}. If the script doesn't define 'output', the node emits null. Downstream edges connect via implicit form ({ "from": "py", "to": "next" }) — the raw value is passed through unchanged.

python_script.default_output_note: default_output is intentionally null. The node returns the raw 'output' value, NOT a { 'output': ... } wrapper. Declaring a default_output of 'output' would make the engine try to extract a non-existent sub-field on every implicit edge — scalar outputs (numbers, strings, booleans) would silently drop to null. With default_output = null the edge resolver passes the raw value through.

llm_call.name: LLM Call
llm_call.description: The core AI node — invokes a language model with conversation memory, tool calling, streaming, and multimodal file support. Sends a prompt to the configured LLM provider and returns the response. Supports three providers (OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic) plus a mock provider for testing. Key capabilities: (1) Conversation memory via session_id + connection_url, allowing multi-turn conversations persisted to PostgreSQL or SQLite. (2) Tool calling via tool_configurations + enabled_tools, letting the LLM invoke other DAG nodes as tools. (3) Streaming via the stream flag, emitting tokens in real-time through the event observer. (4) Multimodal support via the files array, allowing images and PDFs to be sent alongside the prompt. Inputs always take priority over config values, enabling dynamic parameterization from upstream nodes.

provider.description: The LLM provider to use. Determines which API endpoint and protocol is used. See 'llm_shared_fields.provider' for details on each provider.

api_key.description: API key for the LLM provider. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax. See 'llm_shared_fields.api_key' for details.

model.description: Model identifier. See 'llm_shared_fields.model' for details and defaults.

prompt.description: The main prompt to send to the LLM. Can be a string (most common), a JSON array, or a JSON object. Non-string values are automatically serialized to pretty JSON, allowing structured data to be sent as the prompt (useful for the synthesizer pattern where the prompt is an array of task results). Supports '{{variable}}' template syntax resolved against the node's inputs. If the resolved prompt is empty or null, the node is silently skipped (returns null) — this enables conditional execution in multi-turn flows. Falls back to 'task' input/config if 'prompt' is not found.
prompt.example: What is the capital of France?

task.description: Fallback prompt field. Used when 'prompt' is not available in either inputs or config. This enables the orchestrator pattern where tasks are assigned with a 'task' field rather than a 'prompt' field.
task.example: Find the best hotels in Paris for a family of 4

system_message.description: System-level instructions for the LLM. Supports '{{variable}}' template syntax. When 'enabled_tools' is set, the engine automatically appends a tool-use instruction block at the end of this message (listing tool names and rules like 'always use tools for live data', 'never answer from memory'). This means the system_message only needs to describe the agent's role and behavior — no need to manually add tool-calling instructions.
system_message.example: You are a travel expert specializing in European destinations.

temperature.description: Controls randomness/creativity of the LLM's response. Lower values (0.0-0.3) produce more focused, deterministic responses — best for factual tasks, data extraction, and code generation. Higher values (0.7-1.5) produce more creative, varied responses — best for brainstorming and creative writing. Values above 1.5 are very random. Most LLMs default to around 0.7-1.0 when not specified.

max_tokens.description: Maximum number of tokens in the LLM's response. Limits the length of the generated text. One token is roughly 4 characters or 0.75 words in English. If not set, the provider uses its default maximum. Setting this prevents unexpectedly long (and expensive) responses. Must be greater than 0.

max_iterations.description: Consecutive-repeat budget for the ReAct loop guard (since 2026-06-14 this NO LONGER caps total turns). Counts how many times in a row the agent may emit the SAME tool call signature (name + arguments); the count resets the moment it emits a different call. With the default 3: 1st identical call executes, 2nd is nudged (tool not re-executed; prior result + a redirect are returned), 3rd triggers a graceful forced final synthesis (a tool-less LLM call returned as a normal answer) — the agent NO LONGER errors with MaxIterationsReached. The hard ceiling on total turns is separate and NOT graph-configurable (env COLMENA_HARD_TURN_CAP, default 50). Values < 2 behave as 2 (the first call always executes). Raise this only if an agent legitimately needs to repeat the exact same call more times before being redirected.

stream.description: Enables streaming mode. When true, the LLM's response tokens are emitted in real-time through the DAG execution observer as 'LlmToken' events, allowing frontends to display the response as it's generated (typewriter effect). Requires an observer to be configured (automatically available in 'serve' mode). The final result is still returned as a complete string. When false, the node waits for the full response before returning.

enabled_tools.description: Controls which tools are available for the LLM to call. Can be: (1) '*' (wildcard string) — enables ALL tools defined in tool_configurations, (2) An array of specific tool names — enables only those tools, (3) A single tool name string — enables just that one tool, (4) Not specified — no tools available (simple prompt-response mode). The LLM decides when and which tools to call based on the prompt and tool descriptions.

lazy_tool_loading.description: When true, tools in tool_configurations are exposed via a lightweight catalog inside the synthetic describe_tool; full schemas are revealed on demand. Tools with `eager: true` in their ToolConfiguration remain always-on. See developer_guide/29_lazy_tool_loading.md.

secure_suspend_allowed.description: When true, auto-registers a tool named `ask_secret` backed by the `secure_suspend` node. The LLM sees the canonical description and node_schema (a `secrets: [{question, name}]` array) without any entry in `tool_configurations`. Use this as the simplest way to let an agent ask the user for credentials. Explicit `tool_configurations` entries with `node_type: "secure_suspend"` take precedence — the flag is a no-op if the user already declared the tool. See developer_guide/13_security_strategy.md.

attachments_enabled.description: When true (default), this llm_call exposes the synthetic load_attachment tool and contributes any files[] entries it receives to the session-wide attachment catalog. When false, the node still registers its files[] (so other nodes can read them) but the LLM in this node will NOT see the load_attachment tool — use for specialist agents that must not read documents uploaded elsewhere in the session.

summary_enabled.description: Master switch for attachment auto-summary. When true (default), files registered via `files[]` WITHOUT a caller-supplied `description` trigger a one-shot LLM call that generates a one-line description and persists it in `conversation_attachments.description`. The summary call runs in parallel with the main answer call via `tokio::join!`, so it does not add to user-facing latency unless the timeout is hit. Set to `false` to disable auto-summary entirely (callers must provide their own `description` per file, or the catalog falls back to `filename`). The summary call is one-shot and history-less — it does NOT touch `llm_node_history` or count toward conversation memory. Failure modes (extraction error, LLM error, timeout) are silent: `description` stays null and the catalog falls back to `filename`. See developer_guide/31_load_attachment.md for the full pipeline.

summary_max_chars.description: Maximum number of Unicode characters of extracted text sent to the summary LLM after local extraction (PDF via `pdf-extract`, UTF-8 decode for `text/*` mimes). Truncation is char-indexed and safe across multi-byte sequences. The default 5000 ≈ first 2 pages of typical prose, which is enough for the cataloging model to identify document type/topic without paying for the full input. Increase if your documents have important content past the first 2 pages (e.g., long forms where the relevant block is on page 5). Ignored for images — `image/*` mimes are sent whole to the vision model regardless of this value. Char-based (not token-based) for determinism: ~4 chars ≈ 1 token rule of thumb means 5000 chars ≈ 1250 tokens of cataloger input.

summary_model.description: Override the model used for the internal summary LLM calls — BOTH the attachment cataloging summary AND the conversation-history compaction summary (see developer_guide/15_memory_guide.md §'Compactación y recuperación de memoria'). When omitted (null), the engine resolves the cheap tier of the main `llm_call`'s provider via, in order, env `COLMENA_CHEAP_MODEL_<PROVIDER>` then the versioned registry `text/config/cheap_models.yaml` (defaults: Google→`gemini-2.5-flash`, OpenAI→`gpt-4o-mini`, Anthropic→`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`). The summary call always uses the SAME provider as the main call to reuse the single `api_key` — there is no separate provider field. Use this to upgrade the summary quality (e.g., set to `gemini-2.5-pro` when descriptions matter more than cost) or to pin a specific model version; for a global change prefer editing `cheap_models.yaml` or the env var.

summary_timeout_secs.description: Hard per-call timeout (in seconds) wrapping the LLM call inside `LlmAttachmentSummaryGenerator`. If the cheap-tier model takes longer than this for a single attachment, the call is cancelled and that attachment's `description` stays null. The default 15s is generous for Flash/Haiku/4o-mini with ~5000 chars of input (typical p99 < 3s). A SECOND layer of timeout — a batch-level ceiling using the same value — also wraps the entire summary future in `llm.rs::execute` to bound user-facing latency: even if N attachments fan out concurrently and one stalls past the timeout, the batch is dropped and the main answer call returns. Summary tasks run inside a `tokio::task::JoinSet`, so dropping the future aborts all in-flight LLM calls cleanly (no orphaned tasks writing stale summaries after the node returns). Increase if you regularly summarise large PDFs and see false-positive cancellations; decrease for tighter SLAs.

summary_max_output_chars.description: Hard cap on the produced summary's length, in characters. Applied at two layers: (1) the summary prompt instructs the cataloger model to keep its output under this many chars (soft hint to the LLM), and (2) the adapter char-truncates the response post-hoc to enforce the limit regardless of the model's compliance. The default 200 chars fits a one-line description like `"Q3 2026 Financial Report — revenue, expenses, EBITDA"` which is what the `load_attachment` catalog renders per row. Increasing past ~300 starts bloating the tool description shown to the main LLM, which can hurt routing accuracy when many attachments exist. Decrease for very terse catalogs.

tool_configurations.description: Defines DAG nodes that the LLM can invoke as tools. A map where each key is a tool identifier and each value is a ToolConfiguration object. The key can be a semantic name ('search_flights') or a UUID (as generated by frontends) — the engine uses the 'name' field inside the ToolConfiguration as the effective tool name shown to the LLM, falling back to the key only if 'name' is empty. See the 'tool_configuration_schema' section for the complete ToolConfiguration structure.

get_weather.name: get_weather
get_weather.description: Get current weather for a city

skills.description: On-demand markdown skills. Each configured source may be empty. See developer_guide/24_skills.md.

builtin.description: Names of built-in skills compiled into the crate (e.g. 'python-expert'). Optional for layer-2 skills already listed in tool_configurations.<name>.skills — the engine auto-derives those from the tool wiring without needing them repeated here.

paths.description: Paths to skill directories. Auto-detection: if the directory contains SKILL.md at its root it is treated as a single skill; if it does not, every immediate subdirectory that has SKILL.md is loaded as a separate skill (root-of-skills mode, one level only). Relative paths resolve against the directory of the graph JSON file, not the process CWD. Subject to the COLMENA_SKILLS_ALLOWED_DIRS env-var whitelist (colon-separated). See developer_guide/24_skills.md for the full error matrix and references workflow.

session_id.description: A unique identifier for the conversation thread. When provided together with 'connection_url', enables persistent conversation memory — the LLM's message history (system, user, assistant messages) is stored in the database and loaded on subsequent calls with the same session_id. This allows multi-turn conversations where the LLM remembers previous exchanges. If not provided, the node generates a random UUID for a stateless single-turn call. The global '__colmena_session_id' from the DAG state takes highest priority, followed by input override, then config value.

connection_url.description: Database connection URL for persisting conversation memory. Required together with 'session_id' to enable memory. Supports PostgreSQL ('postgres://...' or 'postgresql://...') and SQLite ('sqlite://filename.db' or 'sqlite://:memory:'). The engine uses this URL to create a conversation repository that stores and retrieves message history. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' environment variable syntax. SQLite is good for local development; PostgreSQL for production.

user_request.description:
The original user question or request. When provided, it is prepended to the prompt in the format 'User Request:
{user_request}

---

Agent Results:
{prompt}'. This is the synthesizer pattern — the user_request provides context about what was asked, while the prompt contains the collected results from specialist agents. Useful in orchestrator flows where the final synthesis LLM needs both the original question and the gathered data.
user_request.example: Plan a 7-day trip to Japan in spring

verbose.description: When true, prints the full prompt, system message, and raw LLM response to stdout for debugging. See 'llm_shared_fields.verbose' for details.

files.description: An array of file objects for multimodal LLM input (images, PDFs, documents). Each file can be provided either as a local file path or as base64-encoded inline data. The files are sent alongside the text prompt, enabling vision tasks (describe an image), document analysis (extract data from a PDF), and other multimodal use cases. Each file object requires 'mime_type' and either 'path' or 'data'. Optional fields per entry: 'id' (auto-generated if absent), 'label' (catalog label, falls back to filename), 'description' (short summary added to the catalog line).

mime_type.description: The MIME type of the file (e.g., 'image/png', 'image/jpeg', 'application/pdf'). Must accurately reflect the file format for the LLM to process it correctly.

filename.description: A human-readable filename. If using 'path', defaults to the actual filename from the path. If using 'data', defaults to 'upload.file'. Some providers use this for display purposes.

path.description: Local filesystem path to the file. The engine reads the file contents at runtime. Use either 'path' or 'data', not both.

data.description: Base64-encoded file content, optionally with a data URI prefix (e.g., 'data:image/png;base64,...'). The prefix is automatically stripped if present. Use either 'data' or 'path', not both.

write_to_memory.description: When true, the node writes its result to the task memory database (PostgreSQL) after execution and returns all current tasks in the 'extra_info.all_tasks' field. This is used in orchestrator-managed agent flows where each agent's result needs to be persisted alongside its assigned task. Requires 'task_id' to identify which task to update, and a configured task_memory_repo (available when DATABASE_URL is set).

task_id.description: The UUID of the task to update in the task memory database. Required when 'write_to_memory' is true. Supports '{{variable}}' template syntax to resolve the task ID dynamically from inputs (e.g., '{{task_id}}'). The node writes its LLM response as the task's result in the database.

crdt_documents.description: Optional. When present, the LLM gets v1 synthetic tools for the CRDT documents feature (real-time collaborative xlsx workbooks): crdt_doc_list_sheets, crdt_doc_read, crdt_doc_set_cell, crdt_doc_set_range, crdt_doc_add_sheet, crdt_doc_get_recent_changes (subsystem B), crdt_doc_run_python (subsystem C), crdt_doc_list_sheets_of and crdt_doc_import_sheet (subsystem F — cross-sheet/cross-artifact analysis). Subsystem D (formulas v1) adds server-side Excel-style formula evaluation: values starting with '=' in set_cell/set_range are parsed and evaluated by formualizer with intra-sheet eager recalc; set_cell/set_range return cells_recalculated + structured warnings (needs_browser, eval_error, cycle, parse_error); crdt_doc_read accepts include_formulas to expose {v, f, fs}; crdt_doc_list_sheets returns formula_count per sheet. The artifact_id is required and the LLM never sees it. Three operating modes (descending priority): (1) `ws_url` set → WsPeer mode, the agent opens a WS peer to a remote CRDT documents service (production split topology). (2) `ws_url` omitted, process-wide singleton installed → shared in-process runtime (monolithic deploy / dev convenience via crdt-yws-graph). (3) neither → local autonomous mode, fresh runtime per call backed by `storage_*` fields (plain `dag_engine run`, no live server). Per-tool LLM schemas live in docs/node_as_tools_reference.json under crdt_documents.tool_descriptions.

artifact_id.description: Required. The artifact this llm_call mutates. Format: art_<26-char-ULID>. Static or $DYNAMIC. The LLM never sees it.

ws_url.description: Recommended for production. WebSocket URL to a running CRDT documents service (e.g. 'ws://crdt-service:8090/yjs'). When set, the agent connects as a peer: maintains a local Y.Doc replica synced via Yjs sync v1, propagates mutations to the server which fans them out to browsers and other agents. Disables local storage_* fields (server owns persistence). On WS connect failure the node fails fast — auto-reconnect is deferred to v1.1.

storage_backend.description: Storage backend for local mode (ignored when ws_url is set). 'localfs' stores under storage_root, 'gcs' uploads to a Google Cloud Storage bucket.

storage_root.description: Filesystem root for localfs backend. Ignored when storage_backend='gcs' or when ws_url is set.

gcs_bucket.description: Required if storage_backend='gcs'. The GCS bucket name where document snapshots are uploaded (e.g. 'my-colmena-docs'). Ignored when ws_url is set.

gcs_prefix.description: Object key prefix in GCS. Ignored when storage_backend='localfs' or when ws_url is set.

prompt.description: Dynamic prompt. Takes priority over config prompt.

task.description: Fallback if prompt is not available.

user_request.description: Original user question for synthesizer pattern.

files.description: Dynamic file array for multimodal input.

task_id.description: Dynamic task ID for memory write.

context.<key>.description: Context values accessible in tool_configurations via '${context.key}' template syntax. Used to pass dynamic values (like auth tokens) into tool fixed_config.

result.description: The LLM's text response content. This is the primary output — the generated text from the language model after all tool calls are resolved.

extra_info.description: Metadata about the LLM call including: 'usage' (token counts: prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens), 'tool_calls' (array of tool calls made during execution, if any), and optionally 'all_tasks' (when write_to_memory is true).

information_extraction.name: Information Extraction
information_extraction.description: Extracts structured data from unstructured text using an LLM and a user-defined JSON schema. You provide the schema defining what to extract (field names, types, descriptions), and the node instructs the LLM to output valid JSON matching that schema. The temperature is forced to 0.1 for maximum consistency. Text sources are gathered from: (1) input edges using the 'texts.{name}' pattern (e.g., an edge to 'extractor.texts.email_body'), and (2) static texts defined in config. Multiple text sources are concatenated with headers. If no texts are provided, the node is silently skipped. Can also process critic mutations (add_tasks, delete_tasks) for integration with orchestrator flows.

provider.description: The LLM provider to use for extraction. See 'llm_shared_fields.provider'.

api_key.description: API key for the provider. Supports '${VAR_NAME}' syntax. See 'llm_shared_fields.api_key'.

schema.description: A JSON Schema defining the structure of the data to extract. The LLM is instructed to output JSON matching this schema exactly. Supports standard JSON Schema types (string, number, boolean, array, object) with descriptions for each field. The schema is included in the system prompt, so clear field descriptions significantly improve extraction accuracy. This is the most important config field — it defines what the node extracts.

people_assigned.description: List of people's names assigned to the project

system_message.description: Additional extraction instructions appended to the built-in system prompt. The built-in prompt already instructs the LLM to extract data and output valid JSON. Use this field for domain-specific guidance, like 'Extract dates in ISO 8601 format' or 'If a field is not found, use null instead of guessing'.
system_message.example: Focus on extracting financial figures. Convert all amounts to USD.

texts.description: Static text sources defined directly in config. A map where keys are text source names and values are the text content. Each source is formatted as '# {name}\n\n{content}' and concatenated. In most cases, you'll provide texts dynamically via edges (using the 'texts.{name}' port pattern) rather than in config.

verbose.description: When true, prints the system prompt, texts, and parsed output for debugging. See 'llm_shared_fields.verbose'.

texts.<name>.description: Dynamic text sources for extraction. Use edge paths like { "from": "source.result", "to": "extractor.texts.email_body" }. The node collects all inputs with keys starting with 'texts.' and formats them as labeled text sections. Each text source gets a header '# {name}' for the LLM to reference. Non-string values are serialized to JSON strings.

system_message.description: Dynamic system message override. Appended to the built-in extraction prompt.

result.description: The extracted data as a JSON object matching the provided schema. If the LLM's response contains markdown code blocks, they are automatically stripped before parsing. Returns null if no texts were provided.

output_parser.name: Output Parser
output_parser.description: Parses unstructured text (typically the output of an llm_call or agent) into a structured JSON object matching the provided inline schema. Thin wrapper over the same extraction engine used by information_extraction, with a single 'input' port and inline-required schema declaration. Fails fast on missing input (null, empty string, [], {}) — does NOT silently skip like llm_call does.

model.description: Provider-specific model ID. Falls back to the provider default if absent.

schema.description: Inline-required schema describing the fields to extract. Each property is declared as `{ type, required?, description? }`. Converted internally to standard JSON Schema before being sent to the LLM. Type values: string, number, integer, boolean, array, object.

instructions.description: Optional extra guidance appended to the built-in extraction system message. Useful for domain rules or fallback handling (e.g., 'If you cannot determine the intent, use "unknown".').
instructions.example: If you cannot determine the intent, use 'unknown'.

temperature.description: LLM temperature. Defaults to 0.1 for extraction consistency. Override only if you need creative reformatting.

input.description: The text or value to parse. Non-string values are pretty-printed as JSON before being sent to the LLM.

<schema_fields>.description: The raw extracted JSON object matching the inline schema. NOT wrapped in { output: ... } — downstream nodes read individual fields via dotted paths (e.g., from: 'parser.intent'), or read the whole object by referencing the node id alone (e.g., from: 'parser').

planner.name: Planner
planner.description: An LLM-powered task planner that breaks down a user request into a structured list of tasks with agent assignments and execution phases. The built-in system prompt instructs the LLM to output a JSON array of task objects, each with: task description, assigned agent, completion status (always false), phase number (for execution ordering), and parallel flag (whether it can run concurrently). Agents can be defined with rich metadata (name + description) or as bare strings referencing graph nodes. The planner can also return clarification questions instead of tasks when the request is ambiguous. If tasks already exist in the database for the current session (Turn 2+), the node is silently skipped to avoid redundant LLM calls.

system_message.description: Additional planning instructions appended to the built-in planner system prompt. The built-in prompt already instructs the LLM on task structure, phases, and parallel execution.
